title: Veterinary and Pet Care Business
desc: Start and run a small pet care business, from grooming, boarding and walking to records, hygiene and when to refer to a vet.
outcomes: Explain animal welfare needs and the limits of a non-vet service.
Run safe handling, hygiene and booking steps.
Judge risks, bites, disease and legal duties.
task: Plan and pilot a small pet care service with welfare rules, hygiene plan, booking and price sheet, owner forms and emergency steps.
condition: Practice animals from willing owners or a shelter partner, a spreadsheet, two peers and a mentor veterinarian. Medical treatments are for qualified vets only.
standard: Every pet has an owner form and vaccine record; welfare needs are met; injuries and bites have a response plan; costs and price are shown; peers rate Meets or better.
who: Pet lovers, vet clinic assistants, groomers, walkers and boarders.
evidence: service menu, owner form, hygiene plan, price sheet, pilot log
modules: Welfare basics and the limits of your service
Understand
Every animal has welfare needs, whatever the species. A pet business protects them and knows where its own skills stop.
Learn the five needs: a suitable place to live, a suitable diet with clean water, freedom to behave normally, suitable company or separation, and protection from pain, fear and disease.
Spot stress early: panting, hiding, shaking, pacing, growling, or refusing usual food.
Never leave an animal in a parked vehicle, in direct sun, or without fresh water.
Write which species you accept and which you refuse, since each needs different space and skills.
A walker finds a dog panting hard after 15 minutes in hot weather. She moves to shade, offers water, ends the walk at 20 minutes and shifts later walks to 7 am, then logs the change.
Write a one-page welfare card for two species with one action for each need, plus a list of animals you refuse.
All five needs are covered with no wrong facts, and a mentor vet confirms the card.
Owner forms, consent and records
Apply
You must know the pet and the owner before you accept responsibility. A clear form protects the animal, the owner and your business.
Collect pet name, age, species, vaccine dates, medicines, allergies, behaviour notes, the owner's vet and two emergency contacts.
Get written consent for each service and a signed spending limit for urgent vet care.
Store records securely, share them only when needed, and update them at every visit.
Decline the booking when vaccine proof or contact details are missing, and explain kindly why.

A boarding form for a puppy shows one vaccine dose given 10 weeks ago. The owner is asked to check with the vet and the booking pauses until a vet-signed record arrives. The decision and date go in the file.
Design a one-page owner form, fill it for a practice pet, and write a three-line rule for empty fields.
The form has vaccine, vet, emergency, consent and spending-limit fields, and a peer finds nothing missing.
Safe handling of animals and people
Apply
Most injuries happen when handlers rush, corner a frightened animal or use the wrong gear. Calm, planned handling keeps everyone safe.
Approach from the side, speak softly, let the animal sniff you, and stop if it stiffens, growls or hides.
Match gear to the animal: a fitted harness and lead, a secure carrier, and separate crates for each species.
Before the first job, ask the owner about triggers such as other dogs, loud noise or touch near the tail.
Tell the owner about any bite, scratch or fall the same day, log it, and send anyone hurt to a doctor.
A walker meets a nervous dog near a busy road. She uses a double lead, keeps 3 metres from other dogs, crosses early and rewards calm behaviour. The 30-minute walk ends with no pulling and no bolt.
Practise leading, crating and a calm approach on one practice animal under a mentor, with a five-step observation sheet.
The mentor signs off all five steps as safe, with no injuries and no lasting stress.
Hygiene and disease control
Apply
Clean spaces and hands stop illness spreading between animals. A written routine turns this into habit.
Clean and disinfect kennels, bowls, brushes and tables between animals, using a product made for animal areas and following its label.
Separate at once any animal that coughs, vomits, has loose stools or looks very tired, then call the owner and vet.
Wash hands before and after each animal, bag waste, and keep food in sealed containers against pests.
Keep a signed cleaning log with date, area, method and person.
A boarding dog coughs at 9 am. It is moved to a separate room, the owner is called by 9:10 and the vet by 9:20. Shared bowls and floors are disinfected by noon and each step is logged.
Create a daily and weekly hygiene plan for a small boarding space with a one-week log template.
The plan names task, product type, frequency and person, and a peer can run a day from it.
Knowing when to refer to a vet
Evaluate
A pet business is not a veterinary clinic. You notice problems early, keep the animal safe and bring in a licensed vet quickly.
Phone a vet at once for suspected poisoning, serious injury, trouble breathing, repeated vomiting, seizures, collapse or heavy bleeding.
Do not diagnose or give medicine unless the owner or vet has told you in writing what to do.
Keep your clinic and an out-of-hours emergency number on the wall and in your phone.
Record the time, symptoms and what the animal ate or touched.

A dog eats dark chocolate at 4:05 pm. The carer keeps the wrapper, calls the emergency clinic at 4:10 with the dog's weight, follows the vet's instructions, phones the owner at 4:20 and logs every step.
Write an emergency card with numbers, owner contacts and a six-step action list, then run a timed mock call.
The mock call takes under five minutes, and a mentor vet confirms the card refers serious cases and gives no treatment advice.
Services, capacity and pricing
Analyse
A fair price covers every cost, fits the time and space you really have, and leaves a margin for slow weeks.
List each service and the time per pet, including cleaning, setup and travel.
Add monthly costs: wages, supplies, transport, insurance, space, laundry and advertising.
Divide costs by realistic bookings for break-even, add a margin and compare with nearby prices.
Cap daily numbers so each animal stays safe, for example four dogs per walker.

A groom takes 60 minutes of work plus 30 minutes of cleaning, so 1.5 hours of table time. At 400 INR per staff hour plus 120 INR supplies, cost is 720 INR. A margin of about 50 percent gives a price near 1,100 INR.
Cost three services in a sheet, show break-even bookings per month and set one price each, with currency beside every number.
Totals are correct, the capacity limit is stated, and the price covers cost with a visible margin.
Law, insurance and ethics
Evaluate
Know the rules before your first client. Local law sets licences, insurance and standards, and a licensed professional can confirm them.
Look up the business licence, animal-welfare law, tax and boarding or grooming rules, noting the office or document for each.
Ask an insurance adviser what cover is needed for injury, damage and animals in your care, and file the policy.
Never neglect or harm an animal, and report suspected cruelty to the proper authority.
Advertise only what you deliver, write clear terms and keep owners' details private.

A provider lists four rules for her town, each with the office name and check date. She asks an adviser about public-liability cover, buys it before taking clients and files the policy number and renewal date.
List every rule, licence and insurance need for your place with source and date, and mark items to confirm with a professional.
Each rule has a named source and date, no guess is written as fact, and open questions go to a licensed adviser.
Pilot, review and improve
Create
Run a 30-day pilot with a few clients to prove your service is safe, fairly priced and wanted before you grow.
Take only the clients your plan allows and log bookings, complaints, injuries, near misses and rebookings daily.
Send each owner a short report after every visit with one photo and one fact about the day.
Rank the top three problems by how often or badly they happened and fix each with a date.
Write a 90-day plan for price, capacity, training and one community action.
A pilot records 24 bookings, 2 complaints and 0 injuries. After photo reports begin, rebookings rise from 35% to 55%. The top issue, late pickups, is fixed with a set pickup time on the form.
Present your pilot log, price sheet and 90-day plan to peers and a mentor in a ten-minute talk.
Figures match the log, three fixes are dated, and peers rate the evidence Meets or better.
quiz: Name the five welfare needs.
A suitable place to live, a suitable diet and clean water, freedom to behave normally, suitable company or separation, and protection from pain, fear and disease.
Why do you ask for vaccine records before a booking?
They protect other animals in your care, show the pet has had basic protection and tell you when to ask the owner's vet before accepting the pet.
Name two signs of stress in an animal.
Panting, hiding, shaking, pacing, growling or refusing food; any of these means slow down, give space and tell the owner.
When must you call a vet straight away?
For suspected poisoning, serious injury, trouble breathing, repeated vomiting, seizures, collapse or heavy bleeding; record the time and symptoms.
Can you give a pet medicine on your own judgement?
No. Give medicine only as the owner or vet instructs in writing, because only qualified vets may diagnose and treat.
What belongs on an owner form?
Pet details, vaccine dates, medicines, allergies, behaviour notes, vet and emergency contacts, signed consent and a spending limit for urgent care.
Why separate a sick animal from the others?
It stops infection spreading to other animals; then clean the area, call the owner and vet, and note the actions in the log.
Why should a pet business carry insurance?
It helps cover injury or damage claims involving animals or people; ask a licensed adviser which cover local rules and your services need.
What is table time and why does it matter for pricing?
It is the full time an animal occupies a table or room, including setup and cleaning; it sets how many pets you can serve and what you must charge.
What do you track in a 30-day pilot?
Bookings, income and costs, complaints, injuries and near misses, and rebookings, so fixes and prices rest on real numbers.
rubric: Every claim linked to a dated record and checked by a peer
Checked, dated and explained to others
